e.etymology: A respelling of Cairo, the capital of Egypt, whose Arabic name al-Qahira means the victorious. The K spelling fits the fashion for Kai names.

assoc.t: Cairo, capital of Egypt, by sound

e.etymology: A pet form of Ann and Anna, from Hebrew Hannah (grace, favor). It was a popular given name in its own right in the 19th century.

assoc.t: Annie, red-haired orphan of the comic strip and musical
Annie's organic mac and cheese and snacks

e.etymology: The feminine form of Alexander, from Greek alexo, to defend, and aner, man. Queens and empresses across Europe carried it, including Queen Alexandra of Britain.
From the English word haven, Old English haefen, a harbor, and by extension any place of safety. It came into use as a given name in recent decades.

e.meaning: honor, from Honora; also a short form of Eleanor
e.etymology: A spelling of Nora with a final h, in the style of Hebrew names such as Sarah and Hannah. Nora began as a short form of Honora, from Latin honor, and of Eleanor.

assoc.t: Norah Jones, jazz-pop singer

e.etymology: From the Celtic name Drystan, from drest, riot or tumult, reshaped in Old French romance under the influence of triste, sad. Tristan is the knight who loves Iseult in Arthurian legend.

assoc.t: knight of Arthurian legend, lover of Iseult

e.etymology: A recent American coinage that joins the bird name Wren with the -ley ending of names such as Hadley and Finley.
From French Noëlle, the feminine form of Noël, Christmas, which goes back to Latin natalis, birthday. It is often given to girls born near Christmas.

assoc.t: 2019 Disney Christmas movie starring Anna Kendrick

e.etymology: From the English surname for someone who lived in a lane, from Old English lanu. As an Irish surname it has separate Gaelic sources.

assoc.t: Lane Bryant, plus-size women's clothing chain

e.etymology: The French form of the Frankish name Hludawig, from elements meaning loud or famous and battle. Eighteen kings of France bore it; Lewis, Luis, Ludwig and Luigi are the same name.
namesakes: Louis XIV (king of France, the Sun King)

assoc.t: shorthand for the fashion house Louis Vuitton

e.etymology: A variant of Leila or Lilah, from Arabic layla, night. A separate Indian name comes from Sanskrit lila, play or charm, and lila is the Spanish word for lilac.
The Greek form of Hebrew Shimon, tied to the verb to hear; Simon was also a native Greek name meaning snub-nosed. The apostle Peter was first called Simon.

assoc.t: the children's game Simon Says
Simon, the electronic memory game
the bespectacled chipmunk in Alvin and the Chipmunks
Simon Property Group, the shopping mall owner

e.etymology: One of the most common first names of ancient Rome, probably tied to Mars, the god of war. Mark is the English form of the same name.
namesakes: Marcus Aurelius (Roman emperor and Stoic philosopher)
Marcus Allen (Hall of Fame NFL running back)

e.etymology: From the English surname for someone who lived by an ash tree, Middle English atten ash, with the n carried over onto the tree name. Its use as a first name is modern and American.
namesakes: John Nash (mathematician portrayed in A Beautiful Mind)
Steve Nash (Hall of Fame NBA point guard)

e.etymology: A respelling of the word name Journey, from Old French journee, a day's travel. The -ee ending happens to match the French original.
From Hebrew Yisrael. In Genesis it is the name given to Jacob after he wrestles with an angel, and his descendants and their land took the name from him.
namesakes: Israel Kamakawiwo'ole (Hawaiian singer of Somewhere Over the Rainbow)

assoc.t: the country in the Middle East

e.note: Most people will think of the country first, and the name can draw assumptions about religion or politics.

e.etymology: A K spelling of Chloe, from Greek khloe, a young green shoot, a title of the goddess Demeter. TV personality Khloé Kardashian made this spelling familiar in the late 2000s.

assoc.t: Khloé Kardashian, reality TV star

e.etymology: From the English word faith. Puritans took it up as a virtue name in the 17th century, alongside Hope and Charity.
The English form of the Roman first name Marcus, derived from Mars, the god of war. Mark the Evangelist, author of the second Gospel, spread it through the Christian world.
namesakes: Mark Twain (author of Adventures of Huckleberry Finn)

assoc.t: the Gospel of Mark in the New Testament
a mark, the target of a con

e.etymology: A 20th-century variant of Alana, a feminine form of Alan built on the French form Alain. Alan is a Breton name whose meaning is uncertain.
From Hebrew kohen, priest, the title of the hereditary Jewish priesthood descended from Aaron and the most common Jewish surname. Its use as a first name is recent.
namesakes: Sacha Baron Cohen (comedian who plays Borat)
e.note: Kohen is a hereditary priestly title in Judaism, and many Jewish people find it disrespectful as a first name.

e.etymology: From an English occupational surname, from Old French sailleor, a dancer or acrobat. It sounds the same as the word sailor, which is how most people hear it.

assoc.t: sounds the same as sailor, a ship crew member

e.etymology: The German and Scandinavian spelling of Lucas, from Latin Lucas and Greek Loukas, a man from Lucania in southern Italy. It is the name of the evangelist Luke.
Used in Scotland since the 16th century. Its source is uncertain: possibly Latin orabilis, yielding to prayer, or a variant of Annabel.
A Biblical name: Aziel is a Levite musician in 1 Chronicles, a short form of Jaaziel, from Hebrew words for strength and God.
The Spanish form of Xavier, from the Basque place name Etxeberria, the new house. It spread as a given name in honor of Saint Francis Xavier, who was born there.
The English form of Old French Amee, modern Aimée, from Latin amata, beloved. It has been used in English since the Middle Ages.

assoc.t: Amy's Kitchen organic frozen meals and soups

e.meaning: from an Italian surname, son of Ermanno (army man)
e.etymology: An Italian surname from the given name Ermanno, the Italian form of Herman, army man. American parents took it from the fashion house Giorgio Armani founded in 1975.

assoc.t: Italian luxury fashion house

e.etymology: From a Scottish surname and place name, from Gaelic blar, a field or plain, often a battlefield. Once mostly a boys' name, it is now given mainly to girls in the US.

assoc.t: Blair Waldorf of Gossip Girl
The Blair Witch Project, 1999 horror film

e.etymology: A spelling of Ethan, from Hebrew Eitan, firm or enduring. The Ei- opening follows the Hebrew form of the name.
A spelling of Adeline, a French diminutive of Adele, from Germanic adal, noble. The 2015 film The Age of Adaline gave this spelling a lift.

assoc.t: The Age of Adaline, 2015 film starring Blake Lively

e.etymology: From an English surname for someone who looked after horses, from the word colt. It also serves as a short form of Colton.

assoc.t: Colt firearms, maker of the Colt .45 revolver
Indianapolis Colts NFL team

e.note: Many people hear the gun maker first; the revolver and the AR-15 both carry the Colt name.
